Article 6 §1 of the Convention which, in so far as relevant, reads as follows:

“In the determination of his civil rights and obligations ..., everyone is entitled to a fair ... hearing ... by [a] ... tribunal...”

concepts.interpretation: The Court found a violation of Article 6 § 1 due to disproportionate restriction on the applicants' right of access to a court caused by excessive court fees and refusal of legal aid.

anchor.surface_text: The case originated in an application (no. 52658/99) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by two Turkish nationals, Mr Mehmet Yiğit and Mrs Suna Yiğit (“the applicants”), on 4 August 1999.

concepts.interpretation: The Court examined admissibility including exhaustion of domestic remedies and six-month time-limit under Article 35 § 1.

anchor.surface_text: exhausted the domestic remedies

concepts.interpretation: The Court held that the applicants were not required to initiate criminal proceedings as they chose compensation proceedings, thus domestic remedies were exhausted.

anchor.surface_text: Contracting States enjoy a certain margin of appreciation in that respect

concepts.interpretation: The Court acknowledged the State's margin of appreciation in regulating access to courts but retained ultimate supervisory role.

anchor.surface_text: there is a reasonable relationship of proportionality between the means employed and the legitimate aim sought to be achieved

concepts.interpretation: The Court applied the proportionality test to assess whether the court fees imposed were a justified restriction on access to court.

anchor.surface_text: right of access to a court

concepts.interpretation: The Court found that the applicants' right of access to a court was disproportionately restricted by excessive court fees and refusal of legal aid.

issues.text: Whether the applicants have exhausted domestic remedies before applying to the Court

anchor.surface_text: In their observations, the Government submitted two preliminary objections. In the first place, they maintained that the applicants have not exhausted the domestic remedies and argued that they could have initiated criminal proceedings against the medical staff that operated on their daughter.

issues.text: Whether the applicants complied with the six-month rule for lodging their application with the Court

anchor.surface_text: Secondly, the Government asked the Court to reject the application for non-compliance with the six months time-limit. In their view, the applicants should have lodged their application with the Court following the decision of the Diyarbakır Administrative Court dated 17 November 1998, since decisions regarding legal aid are binding pursuant to Article 469 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

issues.text: Whether the applicants' complaint about denial of access to court due to excessive court fees and refusal of legal aid constitutes a violation of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention

anchor.surface_text: The applicants complained that they had been denied access to a court, invoking Article 6 §1 of the Convention which, in so far as relevant, reads as follows: “In the determination of his civil rights and obligations ..., everyone is entitled to a fair ... hearing ... by [a] ... tribunal...”

issues.text: Whether the requirement to pay court fees amounting to four times the monthly minimum wage constituted a disproportionate restriction on the applicants' right of access to a court

anchor.surface_text: To initiate these proceedings, under domestic legislation, they were required to pay court fees amounting to TRL 180,000,000. At this point, it should be underlined that, in December 1998, this amount was four times higher than the monthly minimum wage in force at the time (see paragraph 23 above). It is also an undisputed fact that, at the time of the events, the applicants had no income.

issues.text: Whether the refusal of legal aid on the ground that the applicants were represented by a lawyer was a sufficient and proportionate reason under Article 6 § 1

anchor.surface_text: Furthermore, it is observed that, when the Administrative Court refused to exempt the applicants from paying the court fees, it referred to the case-law of the Supreme Administrative Court, according to which no legal aid was to be granted to claimants who were represented by a lawyer. The Court recalls that, pursuant to Article 19 of the Convention, its task is not to substitute itself for the competent domestic authorities in determining the most appropriate policy for regulating access to domestic courts.

issues.text: Whether the applicants' other complaints under Articles 3 and 8 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 require separate examination

anchor.surface_text: The applicants complained of the suffering which they have endured because of their daughter's illness, as a result of medical malpractice and the lack of compensation. In this respect, they relied on Articles 3 and 8 of the Convention, as well as Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

arguments.claim: The Court held that the right to a court is not absolute and may be subject to limitations, but such restrictions must pursue a legitimate aim and be proportionate.

anchor.surface_text: 33.�The Court reiterates that the “right to a court” is not absolute. It may be subject to limitations permitted by implication because the right of access by its very nature calls for regulation by the State. Guaranteeing to litigants an effective right of access to courts for the determination of their “civil rights and obligations”, Article 6 § 1 leaves to the State a free choice of the means to be used towards this end but, while the Contracting States enjoy a certain margin of appreciation in that respect, the ultimate decision as to the observance of the Convention's requirements rests with the Court (see Kreuz v. Poland, no. 28249/95, § 53, ECHR 2001‑VI).

arguments.claim: A restriction on access to court will not be compatible with Article 6 § 1 unless it pursues a legitimate aim and there is a reasonable relationship of proportionality between the means employed and the legitimate aim sought to be achieved.

anchor.surface_text: 34.�A restriction placed on access to a court or tribunal will not be compatible with Article 6 § 1 unless it pursues a legitimate aim and there is a reasonable relationship of proportionality between the means employed and the legitimate aim sought to be achieved (Tolstoy Miloslavsky v. the United Kingdom, judgment of 13 July 1995, Series A no. 316‑B, § 59). According to the Court's case-law, a financial limitation may be imposed in the interests of a fair administration of justice.

arguments.claim: The Court concluded that the requirement that the applicants, who had no income, had to pay court fees amounting to four times the monthly minimum wage was disproportionate and violated their right of access to a court under Article 6 § 1.

anchor.surface_text:
38.�Consequently, in the Court's view, the requirement that the applicants, who had no income, had to pay court fees which amounted to four times more than the monthly minimum wage at the time, cannot be considered proportionate.

39.�The Court concludes that in the instant case there has been a disproportionate restriction on the applicants' right of access to a court. There has accordingly been a violation of Article 6 § 1 in that respect.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court found the financial burden excessive and the refusal of legal aid unjustified, thus violating Article 6 § 1.
